effect_name: Aggressive cartoons are funnier
effect_claim: Across six sets of cartoons, higher aggressiveness ratings were positively associated with higher funniness ratings.
effect_claim_quote: The correlation of median humor and median aggressiveness rankings ranged from .49 to .90 in six studies
original_title: More aggressive cartoons are funnier
original_authors: C. McCauley, K. Woods, C. Coolidge, and W. Kulick
original_journal: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
replication_title: Are Aggressive Cartoons Really Funnier? A Replication
replication_authors: Stefan Stieger and Anton K. Formann
replication_target_quote: parent study of McCauley and colleagues (1983)
outcome_quote: Aggressive or painful cartoons were not perceived to be funnier

effect_name: Sight over sound in music competition judgments
effect_claim: With brief clips of music competitions, observers identified winners from silent videos more reliably than from audio-only or audiovisual recordings.
effect_claim_quote: People reliably select the actual winners of live music competitions based on silent video recordings
original_title: Sight over sound in the judgment of music performance
original_journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
replication_title: Sight-over-sound judgments of music performances are replicable effects with limited interpretability
replication_authors: Samuel A. Mehr, Daniel A. Scannell, and Ellen Winner
replication_target_quote: a highly-powered direct replication
outcome_quote: we successfully replicate this finding in a highly-powered sample but then demonstrate that the sight-over-sound effect holds only under limited conditions
review_note: The direct test using the original clips held, while follow-up tests found that the advantage depends on the specific recordings and task.

effect_name: Misery-is-not-miserly effect
effect_claim: In a choice task, sadness increased the cash value participants gave up to obtain a good.
effect_claim_quote: Sadness also carried over, reducing selling prices but increasing choice prices
original_title: Heart Strings and Purse Strings: Carryover Effects of Emotions on Economic Decisions
original_authors: Jennifer S. Lerner, Deborah A. Small, and George Loewenstein
replication_title: The misery-is-not-miserly effect revisited: Replication despite opportunities for compensatory consumption
replication_authors: Nitika Garg, Lisa A. Williams, and Jennifer S. Lerner
replication_target_quote: misery-is-not-miserly effect would replicate
outcome_quote: the effect replicated in the novel context

effect_name: False feedback changes cognitive control's contribution to IAT scores
effect_claim: False feedback that made racial prejudice salient increased the relationship between Stroop cognitive-control performance and race-IAT scores.
effect_claim_quote: increased the relationship with cognitive control (Stroop)
original_title: Manipulating the role of cognitive control while taking the implicit association test
original_authors: Eric F. Siegel, Michael R. Dougherty, and David E. Huber
replication_title: Cognitive Control and the Implicit Association Test: A Replication of Siegel, Dougherty, and Huber (2012)
replication_target_quote: We conducted two direct replications of Study 3
outcome_quote: weak to no support for the original hypotheses

effect_name: Interrogative self-talk advantage
effect_claim: Asking oneself 'Will I?' rather than declaring 'I will' increased goal-directed task performance and intentions.
effect_claim_quote: merely writing Will I as opposed to I will as part of an ostensibly unrelated handwriting task produced better anagram-solving performance
original_title: Motivating Goal-Directed Behavior Through Introspective Self-Talk: The Role of the Interrogative Form of Simple Future Tense
original_authors: Ibrahim Senay, Dolores Albarracín & Kenji Noguchi
replication_title: I Will Use Declarative Self-Talk . . . or Will I? Replication, Extension, and Meta-Analyses
replication_authors: Judy L. Van Raalte et al.
replication_target_quote: self-posed interrogative question ("Will I?") to declarative ("I will")
outcome_quote: found no significant group differences in motivation, perceived exertion, or performance

effect_name: Therapist progress feedback for predicted treatment failures
effect_claim: Giving therapists patient progress feedback improved psychotherapy outcomes for patients predicted to be at risk of treatment failure.
effect_claim_quote: improved outcome relative to patients in the control condition who were predicted to be treatment failures
original_title: The Effects of Providing Therapists With Feedback on Patient Progress During Psychotherapy: Are Outcomes Enhanced?
original_authors: Michael J. Lambert, Jason L. Whipple, David W. Smart, David A. Vermeersch, Stevan L. Nielsen & Eric J. Hawkins
replication_title: Enhancing psychotherapy outcomes via providing feedback on client progress: a replication
replication_target_quote: thereby replicating an earlier study using nearly identical methodology
outcome_quote: improved outcome for clients identified as potential treatment failures

effect_name: Simulated nature restores executive attention
effect_claim: Viewing pictures of natural settings improved directed attention measured with the Attention Network Test relative to urban settings.
effect_claim_quote: viewing pictures of nature can improve directed-attention abilities as measured with a backwards digit-span task and the Attention Network Task
original_title: The Cognitive Benefits of Interacting With Nature
original_authors: Marc G. Berman, John Jonides & Stephen Kaplan
replication_title: Conceptual replication study and meta-analysis suggest simulated nature does not reliably restore pure executive attention measured by the attention network task
replication_authors: Jennifer Adrienne Johnson, Brooke E. Hansen, Emily L. Funk, Francesca L. Elezovic & John-Christopher A. Finley
replication_target_quote: Berman, Jonides, & Kaplan, 2008, Experiment 2
outcome_quote: simulated nature does not seem to reliably restore executive attention

effect_name: Surveillance cues enhance moral condemnation
effect_claim: An image of watching eyes led participants to judge moral violations more harshly than an image of flowers.
effect_claim_quote: Violations were more strongly condemned in a condition where participants were exposed to surveillance cues
original_title: Surveillance Cues Enhance Moral Condemnation
original_authors: Pierrick Bourrat, Nicolas Baumard & Ryan McKay
replication_title: Effect of artificial surveillance cues on reported moral judgment: Experimental failures to replicate and two meta-analyses
replication_authors: Stefanie B. Northover, William C. Pedersen, Adam B. Cohen & Paul W. Andrews
replication_target_quote: effect of artificial surveillance cues on moral judgment
outcome_quote: we found no evidence that artificial surveillance cues impact reported moral judgment
review_note: Four direct experiments found no evidence for the original moral-condemnation effect; the paper's broader meta-analyses reported small or mixed evidence.

effect_name: Sight-word and phonics training improve word-reading fluency
effect_claim: Both sight-word and phonics training increased word-reading fluency in children with dyslexia.
effect_claim_quote: Both sight word training and phonics training had significant effects on word reading fluency
original_title: Sight Word and Phonics Training in Children With Dyslexia
original_authors: Genevieve McArthur, Anne Castles, Saskia Kohnen, Linda Larsen, Kristy Jones, Thushara Anandakumar & Erin Banales
replication_title: Replicability of sight word training and phonics training in poor readers: a randomised controlled trial
replication_authors: Genevieve McArthur, Saskia Kohnen, Kristy Jones, Philippa Eve, Erin Banales, Linda Larsen & Anne Castles
replication_target_quote: quasi-randomised trial of sight word and phonics training
outcome_quote: large and significant valid treatment effect on trained irregular words and word reading fluency
review_note: The word-reading fluency gain held for both training methods, while the sight-word group's reading-comprehension gain did not replicate.

effect_name: Negative testing effect
effect_claim: Retrieval practice reduced later recall of previously studied targets compared with studying those targets twice.
effect_claim_quote: ultimately recalled fewer of those targets compared with a group of participants who studied the targets twice
original_title: The negative testing effect and multifactor account
original_authors: Daniel J. Peterson & Neil W. Mulligan
original_journal: Journal of Experimental Psychology: Learning, Memory, and Cognition
replication_title: Investigating the Replicability and Generalizability of the Negative Testing Effect
replication_authors: Kathryn T. Wissman & Daniel J. Peterson
replication_journal: Journal of Applied Research in Memory and Cognition
replication_target_quote: examining the original demonstration with a novel participant population
outcome_quote: Outcomes establish the replicability of the negative testing effect

effect_name: Imagined immoral contact evokes mental contamination
effect_claim: Imagining a forced kiss elicited more mental contamination than a consensual kiss; a consensual kiss from a moral man elicited the least.
effect_claim_quote: a non-consensual kiss evoked greater feelings of mental contamination than a consensual kiss
original_title: Analyses of mental contamination: Part I, experimental manipulations of morality
original_authors: Corinna M. Elliott & Adam S. Radomsky
replication_title: Mental contamination among people in China: A replication of a moral manipulation experiment
replication_authors: Tan Tang, Zhongfang Fu & Jianping Wang
replication_journal: Journal of Behavior Therapy and Experimental Psychiatry
replication_target_quote: Elliott and Radomsky's experiment (2009)
outcome_quote: Unlike in that study, however, imagining a consensual kiss from a moral man also aroused strong mental contamination
review_note: The forced-versus-consensual contrast held, but the consensual kiss from a moral man produced substantial contamination, unlike the original pattern.

effect_name: Rumination mediates depression-anxiety links
effect_claim: Rumination statistically mediated prospective associations between symptoms of depression and anxiety in adults.
effect_claim_quote: baseline depression predicted increases in anxiety and baseline anxiety predicted increases in depression; rumination fully mediated both of these associations
original_title: Rumination as a transdiagnostic factor in depression and anxiety
replication_title: Repetitive negative thinking as a transdiagnostic factor in depression and anxiety: A conceptual replication
replication_authors: Jolijn Drost, Willem van der Does, Albert M. van Hemert, Brenda W. J. H. Penninx & Philip Spinhoven
replication_target_quote: cross-sectional and prospective relations between anxiety and depressive symptoms
outcome_quote: changes in rumination mediated these associations
review_note: Conceptual replication: the original studied symptom co-occurrence, whereas this paper studied diagnosed disorders; rumination partly mediated the prospective link.

effect_name: Large multivariate sex difference in 16PF personality scores
effect_claim: Across 15 latent 16PF personality factors in a U.S. sample, the original study estimated a large male-female group difference (Mahalanobis D=2.71).
effect_claim_quote: the effect size for global sex differences in personality was D = 2.71
original_title: The Distance Between Mars and Venus: Measuring Global Sex Differences in Personality
original_authors: Marco Del Giudice, Tom Booth & Paul Irwing
replication_title: Global sex differences in personality: Replication with an open online dataset
replication_authors: Tim Kaiser, Marco Del Giudice & Tom Booth
replication_target_quote: an equivalent version of the 16PF
outcome_quote: Our results corroborate the original study (with a comparable if somewhat smaller effect size)
review_note: The replication used an equivalent online 16PF-style questionnaire and found a large multivariate difference, but its D = 2.06 was smaller than the original D = 2.71.

effect_name: Fake news by repetition effect
effect_claim: Repeated statements are more likely than new statements to be judged as having been used as fake news on social media, regardless of their actual truth.
effect_claim_quote: repetition may also increase perceptions that statements are used as fake news on social media
original_title: Repetition increases both the perceived truth and fakeness of information: An ecological account
original_authors: Olivier Corneille, Adrien Mierop & Christian Unkelbach
replication_title: Robustness Tests Replicate Corneille et al.’s (2020) Fake News by Repetition Effect
replication_authors: Jérémy Béna, Olivier Corneille, Adrien Mierop & Christian Unkelbach
replication_target_quote: Corneille et al. (2020, Experiments 1 & 2)
outcome_quote: repeated statements as having been previously used as fake news on social media more than new statements
review_note: Programming errors in the original led to a corrigendum; two preregistered replications with corrected programs reproduced the social-media fake-news judgment effect.

effect_name: Partner success lowers men's implicit self-esteem
effect_claim: Men show lower implicit self-esteem after thinking about a romantic partner's success than after thinking about a partner's failure.
effect_claim_quote: men's implicit self-esteem is lower when a partner succeeds than when a partner fails
original_title: Gender differences in implicit self-esteem following a romantic partner's success or failure
original_journal: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
replication_title: Implicit self-esteem following a romantic partner's success: Three replications and a meta-analysis
replication_authors: Heather-Christina C. Hawkins, Tara L. Lesick & Ethan Zell
replication_target_quote: writing about a romantic partner's success versus failure
outcome_quote: the effect of writing about a romantic partner's success was not statistically significant
review_note: All three replication tests were nonsignificant; the pooled effect was small (d = 0.13), 78% below the original estimate. Two of the three were preregistered.

effect_name: Test-potentiated learning after unsuccessful retrieval
effect_claim: For previously unrecalled items, more practice tests before restudy improve subsequent learning compared with fewer practice tests when trial time is limited.
effect_claim_quote: unsuccessful retrieval attempts enhance the effectiveness of subsequent restudy
original_title: Test-potentiated learning: distinguishing between direct and indirect effects of tests
original_authors: Kathleen M. Arnold & Kathleen B. McDermott
original_journal: Journal of Experimental Psychology: Learning, Memory, and Cognition
replication_title: Test-potentiated learning: three independent replications, a disconfirmed hypothesis, and an unexpected boundary condition
replication_authors: Kathryn T. Wissman & Katherine A. Rawson
replication_target_quote: following more versus fewer practice tests
outcome_quote: more versus fewer tests potentiate learning when trial time is limited
review_note: Three independent replications supported the effect with brief trials; the effect weakened as trial length increased.

effect_name: Skin-tone similarity biases perceived synchrony
effect_claim: Dyads with dissimilar skin tones are judged less coordinated than same-tone dyads even when their actual movement coordination is equivalent.
effect_claim_quote: Participants judged dyads consisting of individuals with dissimilar skin tones to be less coordinated than those with similar complexions
original_title: Perceptions of synchrony: different strokes for different folks?
original_authors: Joanne Lumsden, Lynden K. Miles & C. Neil Macrae
replication_title: Seeing synchrony: A replication of the effects of task-irrelevant social information on perceptions of interpersonal coordination
replication_authors: M. C. Macpherson, N. Fay & L. K. Miles
replication_target_quote: Lumsden, Miles, and Macrae (2012)
outcome_quote: judged dissimilar dyads to be less coordinated than dyads with a similar skin tone
review_note: Preregistered replication with 191 participants; the dyads were objectively matched on movement coordination. One original author joined the replication.

effect_name: Social anxiety prolongs gaze at threatening faces
effect_claim: Adults with social anxiety spend longer looking at socially threatening faces than nonanxious controls in an extended-viewing eye-tracking task.
effect_claim_quote: socially anxious students and participants with SAD dwelled significantly longer on threat faces compared with nonanxious participants
original_title: Social anxiety is related to increased dwell time on socially threatening faces
original_authors: Amit Lazarov, Rany Abend & Yair Bar-Haim
replication_title: Increased attention allocation to socially threatening faces in social anxiety disorder: A replication study
replication_authors: Amit Lazarov, Dana Basel, Sarah Dolan, Daniel G. Dillon, Diego A. Pizzagalli & Franklin R. Schneier
replication_target_quote: Replicating the findings of Lazarov et al. (2016)
outcome_quote: socially anxious patients dwelled significantly longer on threat faces
review_note: The replication used the same extended-viewing eye-tracking task and reproduced longer threat-face dwell time; an original author joined the replication.

effect_name: Peak fertility increases red or pink clothing
effect_claim: Women at high conception risk are more likely to wear a red or pink shirt than women at low conception risk.
effect_claim_quote: women at high conception risk were more than 3 times more likely to wear a red or pink shirt than were women at low conception risk
original_title: Women Are More Likely to Wear Red or Pink at Peak Fertility
original_authors: Alec T. Beall & Jessica L. Tracy
replication_title: Are women more likely to wear red and pink at peak fertility? What about on cold days? Conceptual, close, and extended replications with novel clothing colour measures
replication_authors: Liana S. E. Hone & Michael E. McCullough
replication_target_quote: women's fertility and their clothing choices
outcome_quote: did not find compelling evidence that women are particularly inclined to wear red or pink during peak fertility
review_note: Two studies used self-reports and additional clothing-color measures; the original's fertility association did not hold. The cold-day analysis was an extension.

effect_name: New-decade existential-meaning search
effect_claim: Thinking about entering a new decade of life increases the current search for existential meaning.
effect_claim_quote: adults undertake a search for existential meaning when they approach a new decade in age
original_title: People search for meaning when they approach a new decade in chronological age
original_authors: Adam L. Alter & Hal E. Hershfield
original_journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
replication_title: Thinking about a new decade in life increases personal self-reflection: A replication and reinterpretation of Alter and Hershfield's (2014) findings
replication_authors: Jinhyung Kim, Rebecca J. Schlegel, Elizabeth Seto & Joshua A. Hicks
replication_journal: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
replication_target_quote: replicate their experimental study (Study 2 in their article)
outcome_quote: Studies 1 and 3 replicated their main findings, Study 2 did not
review_note: The three studies targeted original Study 2: two supported its main result and one did not. Reanalysis linked the effect to life review, not perceived value of meaning.

effect_name: Reappraisal affordances predict emotion-regulation choice
effect_claim: Greater opportunity to reinterpret an emotional situation predicts choosing reappraisal rather than distraction, beyond emotional intensity.
effect_claim_quote: reappraisal affordances powerfully influence emotion regulation choice even when emotional intensity and discrete emotions are taken into account
original_title: Emotion regulation choice: the role of environmental affordances
original_authors: Gaurav Suri, Gal Sheppes, Gerald Young, Damon Abraham, Kateri McRae & James J. Gross
replication_title: Reappraisal affordances: a replication of Suri et al. (2018) and investigation of alternate predictors of reappraisal choice
replication_authors: Catherine Nicole Marie Ortner, Maria Stoney & Anna Horst
replication_target_quote: pre-registered replication of study 4 of Suri et al., 2018
outcome_quote: we replicated the original finding that reappraisal affordances predicted reappraisal choice
review_note: The affordance-to-choice link held in a preregistered sample of 315, but the intended high- and low-affordance vignettes were rated in the reverse order.

effect_name: Infants use saliva-sharing to infer close relationships
effect_claim: Infants expect a person observed sharing saliva with another person to respond when that person is distressed.
effect_claim_quote: Toddlers and infants expect that people who share saliva will respond to one another in distress
original_title: Early concepts of intimacy: Young humans use saliva sharing to infer close relationships
original_authors: Ashley J. Thomas, Brandon Woo, Daniel Nettle, Elizabeth Spelke & Rebecca Saxe
replication_title: Do infants use cues of saliva-sharing to infer close relationships? A replication of Thomas et al. (2022)
replication_authors: Beyza Gokcen Ciftci, Jonathan Frank Kominsky & Gergely Csibra
replication_target_quote: replicate their crucial experiment (2B)
outcome_quote: we replicated looking-time preference for the saliva-sharer but did not replicate the tendency to look first to the saliva-sharer
review_note: The looking-time preference held, but the first-look response during distress did not. Testing moved from online to lab, with an eye tracker added.

effect_name: Depression alters sad-versus-happy gaze allocation
effect_claim: In the Matrix eye-tracking task, people with major depression and nondepressed controls differ in how long they look at sad versus happy faces.
effect_claim_quote: patients with MDD and students with high levels of depression dwelled significantly longer on sad faces
original_title: Free viewing of sad and happy faces in depression: A potential target for attention bias modification
original_authors: Amit Lazarov, Ziv Ben-Zion, Dana Shamai, Daniel S. Pine & Yair Bar-Haim
replication_title: Biased attention allocation in major depressive disorder: A replication and exploration of the potential effects of depression history
replication_authors: Shani Lavi, Dana Shamai-Leshem, Yair Bar-Haim & Amit Lazarov
replication_target_quote: Lazarov et al. (2018)
outcome_quote: A significant group-by-stimulus type (happy vs. sad faces) interaction emerged for total dwell time, replicating the findings of the original study.
review_note: The replication abstract reports a group-by-face-type interaction and differences for both face types, but does not specify the direction of the sad-face group difference; success is limited to the interaction. First-fixation measures showed no group effect. Original authors joined.

effect_name: OCD-relevant inverse reasoning
effect_claim: Greater endorsement of inverse reasoning in OCD-related scenarios is associated with obsessive-compulsive symptoms.
effect_claim_quote: greater endorsement of inverse reasoning was significantly associated with OCD symptoms
original_title: Inverse reasoning processes in obsessive-compulsive disorder
original_authors: Shiu F. Wong & Jessica R. Grisham
replication_title: Inverse reasoning processes in obsessive-compulsive disorder: Replication in a clinical sample
replication_authors: Shiu F. Wong, Frederick Aardema & Jessica R. Grisham
replication_target_quote: a task-based measure of inverse reasoning
outcome_quote: the OCD group demonstrated significantly greater endorsement in inverse reasoning on scenarios where OCD relevant concerns were prompted
review_note: Clinical extension of an online-sample association: OCD patients exceeded both control groups on OCD-relevant scenarios; on other scenarios they exceeded healthy controls only. Both original authors joined.

effect_name: Children’s descriptive-to-prescriptive group norms
effect_claim: Children infer that members of a novel group should follow its regular behaviors, evaluating nonconformity more negatively than conformity.
effect_claim_quote: Children negatively evaluated non-conformity, with negative evaluations declining with age
original_title: So It Is, So It Shall Be: Group Regularities License Children's Prescriptive Judgments
original_authors: Steven O. Roberts, Susan A. Gelman & Arnold K. Ho
replication_title: Children's descriptive-to-prescriptive tendency replicates (and varies) cross-culturally: Evidence from China
replication_authors: Steven O. Roberts, Cai Guo, Arnold K. Ho & Susan A. Gelman
replication_target_quote: this descriptive-to-prescriptive tendency in a sample of children
outcome_quote: Like U.S. children, Chinese children disapproved of non-conformity
review_note: The Chinese sample repeated the children's core tendency, with stronger disapproval among younger children and different adult patterns. The discovered candidate linked a separate 2017 follow-up; this is the original paper named by the replication.

effect_name: Safety-aid availability impairs claustrophobia exposure
effect_claim: Making safety aids available during claustrophobia exposure reduces fear improvement compared with exposure without safety aids.
effect_claim_quote: the perception of the availability of safety aids as opposed to their actual use that exerts a disruptive effect on fear reduction
original_title: Disentangling the Effects of Safety-Behavior Utilization and Safety-Behavior Availability During Exposure-Based Treatment: A Placebo-Controlled Trial
original_authors: Mark B. Powers, Jasper A. J. Smits & Michael J. Telch
original_journal: Journal of Consulting and Clinical Psychology
replication_title: Failure to replicate the deleterious effects of safety behaviors in exposure therapy
replication_authors: Jennifer T. Sy, Laura J. Dixon, James J. Lickel, Elizabeth A. Nelson & Brett J. Deacon
replication_target_quote: both the availability and utilization of safety behaviors interfere with the efficacy of exposure therapy
outcome_quote: there were no significant between-group differences in fear reduction
review_note: The 2004 trial favored exposure without safety aids, particularly against aid availability. The 2011 three-arm study found similar fear reduction and improved self-efficacy in the aid-use arm. Its discovered DOI link pointed to a different 2009 paper; the replication explicitly identifies Powers, Smits and Telch 2004.

effect_name: Verbal action-effect instruction priming
effect_claim: Verbal action-effect instructions form associations that prime instruction-compatible responses when the named effect appears.
effect_claim_quote: automatically activated upon encountering the previously verbally presented effect
original_title: Unintentional response priming from verbal action–effect instructions
original_authors: Yevhen Damanskyy, Torsten Martiny-Huenger & Elizabeth J. Parks-Stamm
replication_title: Associative Learning from Verbal Action-Effect Instructions: A Replication and Investigation of Underlying Mechanisms
replication_authors: Yevhen Damanskyy, Torsten Martiny-Huenger & Elizabeth J. Parks-Stamm
replication_target_quote: unintentional response-priming effects from verbal action-effect instructions (direct replication; Condition 1)
outcome_quote: predicted response-priming effect following verbal action-effect instructions (overall conditions and in the replication Condition 1)
review_note: The direct test was Condition 1; the other conditions tested proposed mechanisms and their between-condition contrasts were inconclusive. All three original authors joined the replication.

effect_name: Perceived uncontrollable mortality risk and health effort
effect_claim: Higher perceived uncontrollable mortality risk is associated with less self-reported effort to look after health.
effect_claim_quote: higher perceived extrinsic mortality risk, which in turn predicted lower reported health effort
original_title: Perceived extrinsic mortality risk and reported effort in looking after health: testing a behavioral ecological prediction
replication_title: The Relationship Between Perceived Uncontrollable Mortality Risk and Health Effort: Replication, Secondary Analysis, and Mini Meta-analysis
replication_target_quote: We replicated Pepper and Nettle (2014), who reported a negative relationship between PUMR and health effort
outcome_quote: PUMR was negatively associated with health effort
review_note: This is an observational self-report association, not an intervention. The 2024 socioeconomic mediation estimate was 24%, weaker than the original complete mediation, while the primary negative association repeated. Original author Pepper coauthored the replication.

effect_name: Prescribed optimism in future-outcome vignettes
effect_claim: When advising a person in future-outcome vignettes, participants recommend predictions above the response scale's accurate midpoint.
effect_claim_quote: Optimistically biased predictions were prescribed in each of the eight vignette conditions
original_title: Prescribed Optimism: Is It Right to Be Wrong About the Future?
original_authors: David A. Armor, Cade Massey & Aaron M. Sackett
replication_title: Does performance invalidity undermine replication? Evidence from an undergraduate student participant sample
replication_authors: Melanie A. Mascarenhas & Konstantine K. Zakzanis
replication_target_quote: PVTs were embedded into a direct replication of a 2008 prescribed optimism study
outcome_quote: The effect replicated successfully across the sample (d = 0.98), consistent with the original study (d = 0.93)
review_note: This repeats the original vignette response-scale prescription, not a measured probability forecast. The original already has an earlier counted FORRT attempt; this is a distinct published attempt. The 2026 study was not preregistered.

effect_name: Black female leaders buffered from dominance backlash
effect_claim: In leadership vignettes, displaying dominance instead of communality lowers White women's status ratings but does not lower Black women's ratings.
effect_claim_quote: dominant Black female leaders did not create the same backlash that dominant White female leaders did
original_title: Can an Agentic Black Woman Get Ahead? The Impact of Race and Interpersonal Dominance on Perceptions of Female Leaders
original_authors: Robert W. Livingston, Ashleigh Shelby Rosette & Ella F. Washington
replication_title: Registered Report: Can Agentic Black Women Get Ahead? An Experiment Revisited
replication_authors: Coco Xinyue Liu, B. Ariel Blair & Elizabeth R. Tenney
replication_target_quote: a high-powered direct replication and extension of Livingston et al.
outcome_quote: both Black and White women (as well as men) suffered a status penalty for displaying dominance
review_note: The registered direct replication used N=1,996 online adults and found a dominance penalty for Black women, contrary to the original exception. The original has one earlier counted attempt; this is a distinct published attempt.

effect_name: Conspiracy endorsement anticipates social exclusion
effect_claim: People asked to publicly endorse, rather than criticize, a conspiracy theory expect greater social exclusion, partly through expected negative self-evaluation.
effect_claim_quote: endorsing (vs. criticizing) conspiracy theories about the Charlie Hebdo shooting, led them to anticipate fear of social exclusion
original_title: Stigmatized beliefs: Conspiracy theories, anticipated negative evaluation of the self, and fear of social exclusion
original_authors: Anthony Lantian, Dominique Muller, Cecile Nurra, Olivier Klein, Sophie Berjot & Myrto Pantazi
replication_title: Conspiracy Theories as a Source of Social Stigma in the Age of Corona: A Replication of a Study by Lantian et al. (2018)
replication_target_quote: a close replication of the “conspiracy-theory-as-social-stigma” hypothesis originally tested by Lantian et al. (2018)
outcome_quote: anticipated social exclusion was significantly higher in the endorsement condition than in the rejection condition
review_note: Both studies measured anticipated evaluation and exclusion, not observed social treatment. The close replication changed the topic from Charlie Hebdo in France to COVID-19 in Germany; its main mediation hypothesis was preregistered.

effect_name: Sexual-availability tactics rated best for short-term mate pursuit by women
effect_claim: Observers rate sexual-availability self-promotion tactics as most effective when women seek short-term, rather than long-term, mates.
effect_claim_quote: participants judged sexual availability tactics as most effective when used by women seeking short-term mates
original_title: Strategic Self-Promotion and Competitor Derogation: Sex and Context Effects on the Perceived Effectiveness of Mate Attraction Tactics
original_authors: David P. Schmitt & David M. Buss
original_journal: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
replication_title: Revisiting judgment of strategic self-promotion and competitor derogation tactics
replication_authors: Mons Bendixen & Leif Edward Ottesen Kennair
replication_journal: Journal of Social and Personal Relationships
replication_target_quote: replicate the original findings of Schmitt and Buss
outcome_quote: The pattern of effects for all four self-promotion tactics was clearly in support of Hypothesis 1
review_note: This verdict covers only the sexual-availability self-promotion pattern, confirmed in the author-uploaded full paper's Hypothesis 1 results; some competitor-derogation tactics did not repeat. These are perceived effectiveness ratings, not observed mate-acquisition outcomes.

effect_name: Girls' own-gender brilliance attribution after age five
effect_claim: At age six, girls are less likely than boys to say members of their own gender are 'really, really smart'.
effect_claim_quote: 6-year-old girls are less likely than boys to believe that members of their gender are “really, really smart.”
original_title: Gender stereotypes about intellectual ability emerge early and influence children's interests
original_authors: Lin Bian, Sarah-Jane Leslie & Andrei Cimpian
replication_title: Boys are smart (and really dull and pretty average): Testing replication and validity of the Brilliance Stereotype
replication_target_quote: tested replication of the brilliance stereotype reported in study-1, task (i) of Bian et al. (2017)
outcome_quote: 10-year-old boys and girls both chose own-gender targets as smartest
review_note: The same brilliance-attribution task was tested in children around age ten, whereas the original key result was in ages six to seven. This fails a proposed persistence/generalization of the pattern at ten; it does not directly disprove the original age-six observation.

effect_name: Awe video increases supernatural-control belief
effect_claim: Inducing awe with a nature video increases ratings of supernatural control compared with non-awe control videos.
effect_claim_quote: awe increases both supernatural belief (Studies 1, 2, and 5)
original_title: Awe, Uncertainty, and Agency Detection
replication_title: A series of replication attempts of experimental awe-induction effects
replication_authors: Marianna Graziosi, Alice Chirico, Jeremy D. W. Clifton, Julia S. Rohde, Ria Chhabra & David B. Yaden
replication_target_quote: a direct replication of Valdesolo and Graham’s (2014; Study 1) video manipulation
outcome_quote: there was a significant difference in supernatural control between conditions, though this difference did not hold when compared to the active control condition
review_note: Study 4 used the original videos and outcome items with an online Prolific sample rather than the original campus setting. Awe exceeded neutral on supernatural-control ratings, but not active amusement; the overall three-group test and belief-in-God outcome were null.

effect_name: Low social support increases preference for feminine faces
effect_claim: After a low rather than high social-support prime, women and men preferred feminine facial shape cues more strongly in own- and opposite-sex faces.
effect_claim_quote: low social support priming conditions demonstrated stronger preferences for feminine shape cues in own- and opposite-sex faces
original_title: Social support influences preferences for feminine facial cues in potential social partners
original_authors: Christopher D. Watkins, Lisa M. DeBruine, Anthony C. Little, and Benedict C. Jones
replication_title: Social Support Influences Preference for Feminine Facial Cues in Potential Social Partners: A Replication
replication_authors: Cassidy Sterling, Keesha Kavia, Arianna Cook, Shevaun Adams, and Sara Naboulsi
replication_journal: Journal of Interpersonal Relations, Intergroup Relations and Identity
replication_target_quote: This study is a direct replication of the work done by Watkins and colleagues (2012)
outcome_quote: We did not replicate the finding that femininity is preferred under conditions of low social support.
review_note: The low-versus-high-support prime effect failed; baseline preferences for feminine female faces and masculine male faces remained. The replication used an online autobiographical prime and N = 124.

effect_name: Stigma controllability shapes anger and willingness to help
effect_claim: Compared with physical stigmas, mental-behavioral stigmas were judged more controllable and elicited more anger and less willingness to help.
effect_claim_quote: mental-behavioral stigmas were perceived as onset-controllable, and elicited little pity, much anger, and judgments to neglect.
original_title: An attributional analysis of reactions to stigmas
original_authors: Bernard Weiner, Raymond P. Perry, and Jamie Magnusson
original_journal: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
replication_title: Revisiting Stigma Attributions and Reactions to Stigma: Replication Registered Report of Weiner et al. (1988) With Extensions Examining New Stigmas and Stigma Origin Categorization
replication_authors: Kwan Yin Yeung and Gilad Feldman
replication_target_quote: We conducted a replication and extension Registered Report of Experiment 2 by Weiner et al. (1988)
outcome_quote: We concluded that we found support for the relationship between stigma source and the attribution-affect-help judgment model.
review_note: The core physical-versus-mental-behavioral pattern held, but only 7 of the original 10 stigma-source categorizations matched and four added stigmas showed less uniform patterns.

effect_name: Failure feedback impairs later learning
effect_claim: After binary-choice questions, feedback that an answer was incorrect produced less learning on a later test than feedback that an answer was correct, despite conveying the correct answer.
effect_claim_quote: participants learned less from failure feedback than from success feedback.
original_title: Not Learning From Failure—the Greatest Failure of All
replication_title: Failure to learn from failure is mitigated by loss-framing and corrective feedback: A replication and test of the boundary conditions of the tune-out effect
replication_authors: Nina Keith, Dorothee Horvath, Alexander Klamar, and Michael Frese
replication_target_quote: We conducted two preregistered experiments to replicate the tune-out effect
outcome_quote: The tune-out effect fully replicated in those experimental conditions that represented close replications of the original study
review_note: The close replications supported the original gain-framed, no-correction effect; loss framing and added corrective feedback removed it in extension conditions.

effect_name: Listener holds signal non-understanding
effect_claim: During second-language conversation, a listener's temporary pause in dynamic movement occurred more often in non-understanding than matched understanding episodes.
effect_claim_quote: nonunderstanding episodes were uniquely associated with holds
original_title: The occurrence and perception of listener visual cues during nonunderstanding episodes
original_authors: Kim McDonough, Pavel Trofimovich, Libing Lu, and Dato Abashidze
replication_title: The visual signature of non-understanding: A systematic replication of McDonough, Trofimovich, Lu, and Abashidze (2019)
replication_authors: Kim McDonough, Rachael Lindberg, Pavel Trofimovich, and Oguzhan Tekin
replication_target_quote: This replication study seeks to extend the generalizability of an exploratory study (McDonough et al., 2019) that identified holds
outcome_quote: The association between non-understanding and holds in McDonough et al. (2019) was confirmed.
review_note: The hold association replicated across 35 listeners; the original finding that raters benefited from access to the listener's face did not. Verdict covers holds only.

effect_name: Goal–landmark distance shapes spatial overshadowing
effect_claim: In Clark's nutcrackers, both relative and absolute goal–landmark distance influenced single-landmark search accuracy after training with a four-landmark array.
effect_claim_quote: both relative and absolute goal–landmark distances are important in spatial search.
original_title: Clark's nutcrackers (Nucifraga columbiana) and the effects of goal--landmark distance on overshadowing
original_authors: Aleida J. Goodyear and Alan C. Kamil
replication_title: The effects of goal–landmark distance on overshadowing: A replication in humans (Homo sapiens) of Goodyear and Kamil (2004)
replication_authors: Estibaliz Herrera, Joe M. Austen, and Gonzalo P. Urcelay
replication_target_quote: we aimed to replicate their findings in human spatial navigation by using a virtual environment.
outcome_quote: Landmarks near the goal more effectively overshadowed landmarks far from the goal.
review_note: Conceptual cross-species replication: the original tested birds finding buried food, while the new paper tested humans in virtual navigation; two human experiments found the distance-dependent pattern.

effect_name: MBCT prevents depressive relapse after three or more prior episodes
effect_claim: For recovered patients with at least three prior episodes of major depression, mindfulness-based cognitive therapy reduces relapse or recurrence risk.
effect_claim_quote: For patients with 3 or more previous episodes ... MBCT significantly reduced risk of relapse/recurrence.
original_title: Prevention of relapse/recurrence in major depression by mindfulness-based cognitive therapy
original_authors: John D. Teasdale, Zindel V. Segal, J. Mark G. Williams, Valerie A. Ridgeway, Judith M. Soulsby & Mark A. Lau
original_journal: Journal of Consulting and Clinical Psychology
replication_title: Mindfulness-based cognitive therapy for depression: replication and exploration of differential relapse prevention effects
replication_authors: S. Helen Ma & John D. Teasdale
replication_journal: Journal of Consulting and Clinical Psychology
replication_target_quote: Replicating previous findings
outcome_quote: MBCT reduced relapse from 78% to 36% in 55 patients with 3 or more previous episodes.
review_note: The finding is restricted to recovered patients with three or more previous depressive episodes. The two-episode subgroup did not benefit. The replication includes an original author.

effect_name: Larger reinforcement downshifts predict greater clinical resurgence
effect_claim: During schedule thinning for destructive behavior, larger reductions in alternative reinforcement predict greater resurgence of that behavior when resurgence occurs.
effect_claim_quote: resurgence of destructive behavior increases significantly with decreases in the availability of alternative reinforcement
original_title: Destructive behavior increases as a function of reductions in alternative reinforcement during schedule thinning: A retrospective quantitative analysis
original_authors: Timothy A. Shahan & Brian D. Greer
original_journal: Journal of the Experimental Analysis of Behavior
replication_title: Quantifying increases in problem behavior following downshifts in reinforcement: A retrospective analysis and replication
replication_authors: John M. Falligant, Louis P. Hagopian, Michael P. Kranak & Patricia F. Kurtz
replication_journal: Journal of the Experimental Analysis of Behavior
replication_target_quote: directly apply the analytic procedures described in Shahan and Greer
outcome_quote: positive function ... present in 75% of FCT applications
review_note: Retrospective clinical data: positive association appeared in 8 of 12 applications, close to the original's 80%. It is not a controlled manipulation; the exponential fit is poor when downshifts without resurgence are included.

effect_name: Bowing raises rated facial attractiveness
effect_claim: Bowing portraits receive higher attractiveness ratings than still or backward-leaning portraits of the same 3D human-face models.
effect_claim_quote: mean attractiveness judgment of the bowing portrait was significantly higher
original_title: Effects of bowing on perception of attractiveness
replication_title: Replication of the bowing effect in a web-based experiment
replication_target_quote: whether this effect can be observed in a web-based experiment
outcome_quote: bowing increases the facial attractiveness ... compared to ... standing still
review_note: The web experiment used Japanese participants and 3D human-face models; authors overlap the original study. Publication issue is 2024 (advance online 2023). The 2015 DOI is the foundational effect paper, not the 2021 formal-bowing follow-up.

effect_name: Culture-specific emotional fit predicts well-being
effect_claim: Higher fit between one’s emotions and the cultural norm predicts psychological well-being in culturally central situations: autonomy-promoting situations in the United States and relatedness-promoting situations in Korea.
effect_claim_quote: Psychological well-being was predicted by emotional fit (a) in autonomy-promoting situations at work in the U.S., (b) in relatedness-promoting situations at home in Korea, and (c) in both autonomy-promoting and relatedness-promoting situations in Belgium.
original_title: Feeling right is feeling good: psychological well-being and emotional fit with culture in autonomy- versus relatedness-promoting situations
original_authors: Jozefien De Leersnyder, Heejung Kim & Batja Mesquita
replication_title: Cultural fit of emotions and subjective well-being: Replicating comparative evidence and extending it to the Mediterranean region
replication_journal: Current Research in Ecological and Social Psychology
replication_target_quote: As a conceptual replication of De Leersnyder et al. (2015), we predicted that calculated fit with the normative emotion pattern of one’s cultural group would be linked to better psychological well-being particularly if the fit occurred in culturally central situations.
outcome_quote: only in East Asia calculated emotional fit in culturally central contexts predicted psychological well-being and thriving.
review_note: The 2023 paper separately identifies De Leersnyder et al. (2015) as the H3 target. It conceptually replicates with different situation and well-being measures across 12 countries: the East Asian relatedness-context link appeared, but the expected Anglo-Western individual/autonomy-context link did not. Other hypotheses in this paper target different originals.

effect_name: Overweight body image biases fictional-character portrayals
effect_claim: When college students write about pictured characters, overweight body images lead to more sad or negative stories and less pleasant characters than normal-weight images.
effect_claim_quote: write sad or negative stories, (b) create unpleasant characters ... Support was found for part (a) and (b)
original_title: The Salience of Overweight in Personality Characterization
replication_title: Overweight as Master Status: A Replication
replication_target_quote: The study reported here is a replication of an earlier study exploring association of body image with other personality characteristics.
outcome_quote: In both studies it was predicted that overweight body image would be associated with more negative personality characteristics than normal weight body image, and evidence was found supporting the predictions.
review_note: Same-author replication in college students (original N=223; retest N=290). The original supported negative story tone and unpleasant character depiction, not the semantic-differential personality-scale component. The retest abstract summarizes general support but does not break out every original outcome.

effect_name: Intensive tact teaching increases spontaneous tacts
effect_claim: For preschool children with autism, 100 additional daily tact learning opportunities increased spontaneous tacts in settings outside instruction.
effect_claim_quote: The intervention increased vocal verbal operants (tacts and mands) emitted by the target students in NIS.
original_title: The Effects of Daily Intensive Tact Instruction on Preschool Students' Emission of Pure Tacts and Mands in Non-Instructional Setting
original_authors: Nirvana Pistoljevic and R. Douglas Greer
original_journal: Journal of Early and Intensive Behavior Intervention
replication_title: The effects of intensive tact instruction with young children having speech delays on pure tacts and mands in non-instructional settings: a partial replication
replication_authors: Jeremy H. Greenberg, Wendy Tsang, and Tracy Yip
replication_target_quote: The purpose of the current study was to replicate the original research findings conducted by Pistoljevic & Greer (2006)
outcome_quote: All three students were observed to emit significantly more tacts after mastering the 100 learn units through the intensive tact instruction.
review_note: Partial protocol replication in three older children with autism in Hong Kong (ages 6–9 rather than 3–4); spontaneous tacts increased in all three, while mands increased in only two.

effect_name: Health anxiety tracks lower quality of life in MS
effect_claim: Among patients with relapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis, those with higher health anxiety reported lower quality of life even after accounting for disability.
effect_claim_quote: The high health anxiety group reported poorer QoL relative to the other groups, independent of level of disability.
original_title: The impact of health anxiety in patients with relapsing remitting multiple sclerosis: Misperception, misattribution and quality of life
original_authors: Aimee L. Hayter, Paul M. Salkovskis, Eli Silber, and Robin G. Morris
replication_title: The Impact of Health Anxiety in Multiple Sclerosis: A Replication and Treatment Case Series
replication_authors: Neil Carrigan, Leon Dysch, and Paul M. Salkovskis
replication_target_quote: Study 1 sought to replicate the main findings from Hayter et al. (2016).
outcome_quote: This effect remained significant even when level of physical disability (GNDS) was controlled using ANCOVA
review_note: Study 1 tested only 20 MS patients and reproduced the quality-of-life association. Subjective cognitive-performance difference held; physical-performance and attribution-to-MS differences did not. The separate four-person CBT case series is excluded from this verdict.

original_title: Errors in Training Computer Skills: on the Positive Function of Errors
replication_title: Error training: Replication and the function of exploratory behavior
effect_name: Error training improves computer-skill performance
effect_claim: Trainees who practiced computer skills with induced errors outperformed error-avoidance trainees on later nonspeed tests.
effect_claim_quote: The error-training group showed higher scores in the nonspeed performance tests.
original_authors: Michael Frese, Felix Brodbeck, Torsten Heinbokel, Christina Mooser, Erik Schleiffenbaum, and Petra Thiemann
replication_target_quote: replicated and extended the findings of Frese et al. (1991) on the superiority of error training
outcome_quote: The error training group performed better than the group that received training in which they were not allowed to make any errors.
review_note: The original computer-skills study used 24 trainees; the follow-up used 30 psychology students. This verdict concerns later performance, not whether errors themselves caused greater exploration.

original_title: Comparing Leaders' Ratings to Targets' Self-Reported Resistance to Task Assignments: An Extension of Chester Barnard's Zones of Indifference
replication_title: Leaders' Anticipated and Targets' Self-Reported Resistance to Task Assignments: A Replication
effect_name: Leaders overestimate resistance to assigned tasks
effect_claim: Leaders rated assigned tasks as less enjoyable and more likely to be resisted than the targets themselves reported.
effect_claim_quote: leaders rated the tasks they assigned to targets as less enjoyable, undesirable, more above the call of duty, and more likely to be resisted than targets self-reported.
replication_authors: John E. Barbuto Jr., Susan M. Fritz, and Brent J. Goertzen
replication_target_quote: This is a follow up study of Barbuto's 2000 work in which leaders' ratings and targets' self-reported resistance to task assignments are compared.
outcome_quote: leaders tend to underestimate followers' willingness to perform assigned tasks.
review_note: The follow-up uses 650 leader-member dyads versus the original 201 leaders and targets; it confirms the direction of the perceived-resistance gap. A second discovery deposit uses the alternate DOI 10.2466/pr0.90.2.515-520 for this same 2002 article; the alias is not a valid duplicate_candidate_id under the current exact-DOI rule.

original_title: Subliminal influence on preferences? A test of evaluative conditioning for brief visual conditioned stimuli using auditory unconditioned stimuli
replication_title: No evaluative conditioning effects with briefly presented stimuli
effect_name: Brief visual-auditory pairing may shift preferences
effect_claim: A preregistered cross-modal experiment found tentative preference change after 20 ms visual stimuli were paired with valued auditory stimuli.
effect_claim_quote: we found some indication for an EC effect for CSs presented for 20 ms.
original_authors: Tobias Heycke, Frederik Aust, and Christoph Stahl
replication_target_quote: The present study realized a close replication of this study
outcome_quote: Overall EC for briefly presented stimuli was absent
review_note: The original 20 ms effect was small, tentative, and not robust in exploratory analyses. The close replication changed stimuli, added practice, and tested visibility; any detected conditioning required above-chance identification.

original_title: Self‐Reported Beliefs About Verbal Cues Correlate with Deception‐Detection Performance
replication_title: I Told You So! Verbal cue beliefs are associated with truth detection, but not lie detection
effect_name: Verbal-cue knowledge tracks recognition of truthful accounts
effect_claim: People with more accurate beliefs about verbal deception cues gave more accurate credibility ratings to truthful statements.
effect_claim_quote: a better insight in verbal cues was related to an increased accuracy for identifying truthful statements
original_authors: Glynis Bogaard and Ewout H. Meijer
replication_authors: Glynis Bogaard, Sarah Elizabeth Fieweger, and Ewout H. Meijer
replication_target_quote: replicate and extend previous findings on the relationship between accurate beliefs about the diagnosticity of verbal deception cues
outcome_quote: a small but significant positive correlation between accurate verbal cue beliefs and the credibility ratings of truthful, but not deceptive, statements.
review_note: The original first appeared online in 2017 and in a 2018 issue. The preregistered follow-up confirms only a small association for truthful statements; neither study supports improved lie detection.

original_title: Low Trait Self-Control in Problem Gamblers: Evidence from Self-Report and Behavioral Measures
replication_title: Gambling Increases Self-Control Strength in Problem Gamblers
effect_name: Problem gamblers show lower self-control
effect_claim: Higher-risk gamblers scored lower than lower-risk gamblers on self-report and behavioral measures of self-control.
effect_claim_quote: compared to lower-risk gamblers, higher-risk gamblers have relative trait self-control deficits.
original_authors: Anne E. Bergen, Ian R. Newby-Clark, and Andrea Brown
replication_authors: Anne E. Bergen, Ian R. Newby-Clark, and Andrea Brown
replication_target_quote: Replicating Bergen et al. (J Gambl Stud, doi: 10.1007/s10899-011-9274-9, 2011)
outcome_quote: control condition participants categorized as problem gamblers persisted for less time than did lower gambling risk participants.
review_note: The later study replicated the lower self-control contrast in its control conditions in two experiments. Its separate finding that slot-machine play temporarily raised persistence is excluded from this verdict.

original_title: Unsuccessful retrieval attempts enhance subsequent learning.
original_journal: Journal of Experimental Psychology Learning Memory and Cognition
replication_title: Effects of making errors in learning a foreign language
effect_name: Unsuccessful retrieval attempts can improve later learning
effect_claim: Trying and failing to retrieve an answer before feedback improved subsequent learning relative to reading the answer without a retrieval attempt.
effect_claim_quote: Unsuccessful retrieval attempts enhanced learning with both types of materials.
original_authors: Nate Kornell, Matthew Jensen Hays, and Robert A. Bjork
replication_target_quote: We sought to replicate the finding using educationally relevant stimuli.
outcome_quote: Overall there was evidence that errorful training produced superior learning of the meaning and grammar of the foreign language sentences.
review_note: This is a conceptual extension from fictional facts and weak associates to foreign-language sentences. The later experiments provided immediate feedback after incorrect translations.

original_title: The development of children's theory of mind: The working memory explanation
replication_title: Working memory and children's developing understanding of mind
effect_name: Working memory predicts preschool false-belief understanding
effect_claim: Among preschoolers, backward digit span predicted false-belief task performance after accounting for age and vocabulary.
effect_claim_quote: BDS significantly predicted performance on both the false belief and false photograph tasks with age and PPVT-R score controlled
original_authors: Helen L. Davis and Chris Pratt
replication_authors: Thomas Keenan, David R. Olson, and Zopito Marini
replication_target_quote: A major goal of the study was to replicate the findings of Davis and Pratt using a wider set of false belief tasks
outcome_quote: when the effects of age were controlled for, working memory accounted for 7.4% of the variance in children's false belief scores.
review_note: The follow-up used a different working-memory measure and broader false-belief battery; it controlled age but the abstract does not say it also controlled vocabulary.

original_title: Children's Understanding of the Distinction between Real and Apparent Emotion
replication_title: Japanese Children's Understanding of the Distinction Between Real and Apparent Emotion
effect_name: Older preschoolers better distinguish felt from displayed emotion
effect_claim: Six-year-olds distinguished a story character's real emotion from the emotion the character displayed more reliably than four-year-olds.
effect_claim_quote: 6-year-olds demonstrated their grasp of the difference between real and apparent emotion
original_authors: Paul L. Harris, K. Donnelly, G. R. Guz, and R. Pitt-Watson
replication_authors: D. Gardner, Paul L. Harris, M. Ohmoto, and T. Hamazaki
replication_target_quote: investigated in a replication of Harris, Donnelly, Guz and Pitt-Watson (1986)
outcome_quote: 6-year-olds understand the distinction between real and apparent emotion more systematically than 4-year-olds.
review_note: The later study examined Japanese children with the original story approach. The original also found limited understanding among four-year-olds; the verdict is limited to the age contrast.

original_title: The Love of Large Numbers: A Popularity Bias in Consumer Choice
replication_title: The Love of Large Numbers Revisited: A Coherence Model of the Popularity Bias
effect_name: Many reviews bias consumer choice toward popular products
effect_claim: When comparing online product reviews, people sometimes favored an item with more reviews even when a statistical model favored the less-reviewed item.
effect_claim_quote: people preferred a product with more reviews to one with fewer reviews even though the statistical model indicated that the latter was likely to be of higher quality
original_authors: Derek Powell, Jingqi Yu, Melissa DeWolf, and Keith J. Holyoak
replication_authors: Daniel W. Heck, Lukas Seiling, and Arndt Bröder
replication_target_quote: we reanalyzed the data of Powell and colleagues and ran an online study with 244 participants
outcome_quote: Besides replicating the popularity bias, the study provided clear evidence for the predicted coherence effect
review_note: The later online study used a wider stimulus range and additionally tested a coherence model. First published online December 2019; issue dated February 2020.

original_title: Infant Crying and Maternal Responsiveness
replication_title: Are infant crying and maternal responsiveness during the first year related to infant-mother attachment at 15 months?
effect_name: Prompt maternal response predicts less later infant crying
effect_claim: In a longitudinal infant sample, consistent and prompt maternal responses were associated with less frequent and shorter later crying.
effect_claim_quote: consistency and promptness of maternal response is associated with decline in frequency and duration of infant crying.
original_authors: Silvia M. Bell and Mary D. Salter Ainsworth
replication_authors: Marinus H. van IJzendoorn and Frans O. A. Hubbard
replication_target_quote: Bell and Ainsworth's (1972) Baltimore study on maternal responsiveness, infant crying and infant attachment security was replicated and extended.
outcome_quote: the more frequently mothers ignored their infants' crying bouts in the first nine-week period, the less frequently their infants cried
review_note: The later 50-family study found similar descriptive crying patterns but opposite early-period association for maternal ignoring and subsequent crying; this verdict addresses that directional responsiveness claim, not all findings in either paper.

original_title: Your Understanding Is My Understanding
replication_title: You Understand, So I Understand: How a “Community of Knowledge” Shapes Trust and Credibility in Expert Testimony Evidence
replication_authors: Ashley C. T. Jones & Morgan R. Haga
effect_name: Borrowed expert understanding boosts felt understanding
effect_claim: People rate their own understanding of unfamiliar phenomena higher when told scientists understand them, even without receiving an explanation.
effect_claim_quote: people rated their own understanding of novel natural phenomena as higher when they were told that scientists understood the phenomena
replication_target_quote: Study One replicated original CK effect studies in a jury-eligible M-Turk sample
outcome_quote: the original CK effect was replicated
review_note: Study 1 used the original stimuli and new stimuli in a jury-eligible online sample; the separate courtroom extension is not needed for this verdict.

original_title: Embodied Grounding of Memory: Toward the Effects of Motor Execution on Memory consolidation
original_authors: Willem O. van Dam, Shirley-Ann Rueschemeyer, Harold Bekkering & Oliver Lindemann
replication_title: Absence of post-learning motor activity effects on memory for motor-related words
replication_authors: Tatiana Romero, Cecilia Alejandra Vargas, María Ángeles Alonso, Emiliano Díez & Angel Fernandez
effect_name: Congruent motor actions enhance action-word memory
effect_claim: Performing a motor action during the retention interval improves later recognition of action-related words whose function matches that action.
effect_claim_quote: a better memory for words that denoted objects for which the functional use was congruent with the action performed during the retention interval
replication_target_quote: Two of the experiments ... exactly and independently replicated the experimental design and conditions of the original experiment.
outcome_quote: Yes/No recognition scores plus additional analysis of response times showed no motor consolidation effects.
review_note: The two close replications (n=30 and n=44) both found null effects; two extension experiments were also null. DOI year and online date are 2020; print issue appeared in 2022.

original_title: Prevalence of Malingering in Inpatient Suicide Ideators and Attempters
replication_title: Prevalence of Malingering in Suicidal Psychiatric Inpatients: A Replication
replication_authors: D. A. Rissmiller, R. A. Steer, M. Friedman & R. DeMercurio
effect_name: About one in ten suicidal inpatients report malingering
effect_claim: Approximately 10% of psychiatric inpatients admitted for suicidal thoughts or attempts anonymously report deliberately exaggerating or feigning suicidality.
effect_claim_quote: Four patients (10%) indicated they had malingered
replication_target_quote: Prevalence of malingering in suicidal psychiatric inpatients: a replication
outcome_quote: 6 (12%) of the inpatients reported malingering. This rate was comparable to the 10% rate which had previously been found
review_note: Both small hospital samples used anonymous self-report, original 4/40 and replication 6/50. This is a descriptive prevalence comparison, not proof of a stable population rate.

original_title: A disrupt-then-reframe technique of social influence.
original_authors: Barbara Price Davis & Eric S. Knowles
replication_title: Disrupt-Then-Reframe is in the Air: A French Replication and Refinement
replication_authors: Roxane Saint-Bauzel, Audrey Pelt, Laura Barbier & Valérie Fointiat
original_journal: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
effect_name: Disrupt then reframe raises purchase compliance
effect_claim: In charity card sales, stating the price in an unexpected unit and then reframing it as a bargain increases purchases compared with a standard request.
effect_claim_quote: Four studies showed that a disrupt-then-reframe (DTR) technique was influential in getting household residents to purchase cards supporting a local charity.
replication_target_quote: verify that this technique ... could be effective in a French context
outcome_quote: when the two phases of the technique are linked, a greater persuasive effect is observed
review_note: The French field experiment used charity card purchases and compared the complete sequence with standard, disruption-only, and reframe-only scripts; this is a cross-cultural extension.

original_title: Behavior as seen by the actor and as seen by the observer.
original_authors: Richard E. Nisbett, Craig Caputo, Patricia Legant & Jeanne Marecek
replication_title: Actor-Observer Differences in Attribution: A Replication
original_journal: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
effect_name: People explain their own choices more situationally than a friend's
effect_claim: In explaining choices of partner and college major, people describe their own choices using situation or option properties more than they do for a best friend's choices.
effect_claim_quote: describe their best friend's choices ... in terms referring to dispositional qualities ... while more often describing their own similar choices in terms of properties of the girlfriend or major
replication_target_quote: Nisbett, et al., (1973) presented evidence that male actors use more situational than dispositional explanations for their own behavior
outcome_quote: Situational attributions are made primarily to the self.
review_note: The original male pattern held in 41 male actors and appeared in 41 female actors. The replication cautions that dispositional attributions were equal for self and friend; this verdict covers the extra situational explanations for self, not the broad actor-observer theory.

original_title: Cognitive gains in 7-month-old bilingual infants
replication_title: Is mere exposure enough? The effects of bilingual environments on infant cognitive development
replication_authors: Dean D'Souza, Donna Brady, Julia Haensel & Hana D'Souza
original_journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
effect_name: Bilingual infants reverse a learned visual response faster
effect_claim: After a visual cue changes reward location, seven-month-old bilingual infants redirect anticipatory looks while matched monolingual infants do not.
effect_claim_quote: only bilinguals succeeded in redirecting their anticipatory looks when the cue began signaling the reward on the opposite side
replication_target_quote: To confirm the bilingual advantage in infants ... we administered four gaze-contingent eye-tracking tasks
outcome_quote: We could not replicate the finding by Kovacs and Mehler that bilingual but not monolingual infants inhibit learned behaviour (experiment 1).
review_note: The close task (experiment 1; bilingual n=51, monolingual n=51 across study) failed. Other tasks showed exploratory attention differences; those do not rescue this exact response-reversal result.

original_title: Some Exploratory Findings on the Development of Musical Tastes
original_authors: Morris B. Holbrook & Robert M. Schindler
replication_title: Farewell to Holbrook & Schindler’s (1989) “Song-Specific Age”? – Little Evidence for Lifelong Influence of Age-Specific Musical Preferences
replication_authors: Reinhard Kopiez, Jan Weigang, Friedrich Platz & Nina Düvel
effect_name: Popular-music liking peaks for songs from age twenty-four
effect_claim: Adults' later liking of popular songs peaks for songs released when they were about 24 years old.
effect_claim_quote: the development of tastes for popular music follows an inverted U-shaped pattern that reaches a peak in about the 24th year
replication_target_quote: In this replication study, N = 162 participants ... indicated their preferences for 18 song excerpts
outcome_quote: the original finding of an SSA peak in the phase of early adulthood (23.47 years) could not be confirmed in terms of a point estimate
review_note: German chart songs and N=162 produced an overall estimated peak at 14.16 years; the 50+ subgroup was near 22.63 with weak fit. Verdict concerns the proposed single peak around 24, not all music-related reminiscence.

original_title: A Spontaneous Self-Reference Effect in Memory: Why Some Birthdays Are Harder to Remember Than Others
replication_title: The effect of spontaneous self-reference on memory: A replication
replication_authors: Serge Brédart, Sarah François & Serge Guimond
effect_name: Birth-month proximity improves memory for other birthdays
effect_claim: People more readily remember another person's birth month when it is close to their own birth month.
effect_claim_quote: participants were more likely to remember the birthday of a friend if the friend's birthday was close to their own
replication_target_quote: aimed at replicating Kesebir and Oishi's ... spontaneous self-reference effect on memory for birthday dates
outcome_quote: The spontaneous self-reference effect was replicated using the dependent measure that Kesebir and Oishi used in their original study
review_note: Institutional published-version record lists DOI 10.4074/S0003503313002017 while discovery uses its 10.3917/anpsy.132.0161 DOI for the same 2013 article. The study reproduced the own-month proximity measure and also found a recall-proportion effect.

effect_name: Habit reversal for public-speaking filled pauses
effect_claim: Simplified habit reversal training, combining awareness and a competing response, immediately reduced filled pauses during public speaking in six participants.
effect_claim_quote: During postintervention assessments, all 6 participants exhibited an immediate decrease in filled pauses.
original_title: Using habit reversal to decrease filled pauses in public speaking
original_authors: Carolyn Mancuso and Raymond G. Miltenberger
replication_title: Habit Reversal to Decrease Filled Pauses in Public Speaking: A Partial Replication
replication_target_quote: Mancuso and Miltenberger used habit reversal to decrease filled pauses in public speaking. The present study aimed at replicating this study as a student project.
outcome_quote: The mean number of responses (filled pauses) per minute decreased throughout the study and during follow-up measurement.
review_note: Both OpenAlex primary fields are Psychology. The replication shortened training in four social-work students. Although filled pauses declined, three of four participants were already declining at baseline, so the authors said experimental control was not replicated. Original article was online in 2015 and 2016 issue; replication online in 2019 and 2020 issue.

effect_name: Childhood sexual abuse and earlier female puberty
effect_claim: Sexually abused adolescent girls in a small matched sample were more likely to have matured early than girls without reported sexual abuse.
effect_claim_quote: Sexually abused girls were more likely to be early maturers than were non-abused girls; they also felt significantly older than did their non-abused chronological agemates.
original_title: Sexual abuse, pubertal timing, and subjective age in adolescent girls: A research note
original_authors: P. K. Turner, M. G. Runtz, and N. L. Galambos
original_journal: Journal of Reproductive and Infant Psychology
replication_title: Early Childhood Maltreatment and Pubertal Development: Replication in a Population-Based Sample
replication_authors: Jane Mendle, Rebecca M. Ryan, and Kirsten M. McKone
replication_target_quote: In addition to replicating results from smaller, more specialized samples, these findings reinforce the value of considering puberty within a broader “life span” continuum of birth to adolescence.
outcome_quote: Child sexual abuse predicted earlier menarche and development of secondary sexual characteristics, whereas other types of maltreatment did not.
review_note: Both OpenAlex primary fields are Psychology. The 2016 population-based study explicitly cites Turner, Runtz, and Galambos (1999) among prior smaller samples and tests the same abuse-earlier-puberty association in 6,273 girls. It does not retest subjective age and does not establish causation. Online publication of replication was 2015; issue year was 2016.

effect_name: Guided imagery and lung function in asthmatic schoolchildren
effect_claim: A school-based relaxation and guided-imagery program improved forced expiratory volume in one second in four middle-school students with asthma.
effect_claim_quote: With the introduction of the intervention, it was found that FEV1 improved and anxiety decreased in all students.
original_title: Relaxation and guided imagery: A school-based intervention for children with asthma
original_authors: Heather L. Peck, Melissa A. Bray, and Thomas J. Kehle
replication_title: Relaxation and guided imagery as an intervention for children with asthma: A replication
replication_authors: Robin L. Dobson, Melissa A. Bray, Thomas J. Kehle, Lea A. Theodore, and Heather L. Peck
replication_target_quote: The current study served as a replication and extension of this previous research.
outcome_quote: Results demonstrated that RGI significantly improved the lung functioning of 3 out of 4 participants in the study.
review_note: Both OpenAlex primary fields are Psychology. Original tested four middle-school students and reported improved FEV1 in all four; replication tested four elementary pupils and reported improved lung function in three. Its abstract does not break the lung-function outcome out by FEV1 versus other spirometry, so the original-specific metric should not be claimed as directly reproduced. Anxiety effects varied: state anxiety fell in 2/4, trait anxiety in 4/4.

effect_name: Meaning-centered intervention increases life meaning
effect_claim: Among undergraduate women with high weight and shape concerns, six weekly meaning-centered psychotherapy sessions increased reported life meaning compared with a waitlist after treatment and at four-week follow-up.
effect_claim_quote: Participants in the experimental condition showed a stronger increase in meaning than participants in the waiting-list condition after the intervention and at follow-up.
original_title: The Effects of a Meaning-Centered Intervention on Meaning in Life and Eating Disorder Symptoms in Undergraduate Women With High Weight and Shape Concerns: A Randomized Controlled Trial
original_authors: Sanne F. W. van Doornik, Klaske A. Glashouwer, Brian D. Ostafin, and Peter J. de Jong
replication_title: A Meaning-Centered Intervention for Undergraduate Women With High Weight and Shape Concerns—Replication of a Randomized Controlled Trial
replication_authors: Franziska Schutzeichel, Marije aan het Rot, Sanne F. W. van Doornik, Klaske A. Glashouwer, Mirjam I. Frey, and Peter J. de Jong
replication_target_quote: This study was part of a larger project with two aims (AsPredicted #111500, https://aspredicted.org/BCC_F93). This article addresses the first aim of replicating an RCT by van Doornik et al. (2024), assessing the efficacy of a meaning-centered intervention, including the critical measures that were assessed in the original study.
outcome_quote: Compared to the waitlist condition (n = 68), participants in the intervention condition (n = 63) again scored higher on the presence of life meaning at post-assessment and follow-up.
review_note: Both OpenAlex primary fields are Psychology. The replication preregistered its main comparison at AsPredicted #111500 and repeated the original online six-session intervention after COVID distancing ended. Both support increased life meaning, while the replication found eating-disorder symptom reduction only at higher baseline severity; the verdict covers life meaning only. Original DOI went online June 2023 but appeared in the January 2024 journal issue. A 2024 corrigendum corrected the original psychological-well-being scale scoring but did not change interpretation of that secondary effect.

original_title: Teaching Receptive Vocabulary to Minimally Verbal Preschoolers With Autism Spectrum Disorder: A Single-Case Multiple Baseline Design
replication_title: Teaching receptive vocabulary to two autistic children: A replicated, clinic-based, single case experimental design
effect_name: Match-to-sample vocabulary generalization in autistic preschoolers
effect_claim: After matching objects to identical pictures, autistic preschoolers identify taught objects and generalize to new pictures.
